claim: Human running is often modeled as being periodic.
source: Human running is often modeled as being periodic (Blickhan and Full, 1993; Seyfarth et al., 2002; Srinivasan and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature that models running as periodic.

claim: Running is not exactly periodic, even on a treadmill at constant speed.
source: But running is not exactly periodic, even on a treadmill at constant speed.
evidence: This is a general observation that sets up the study's focus on variability.

claim: Body motion during running varies from step to step.
source: Body motion during running varies from step to step (Cavanagh et al., 1977; Belli et al., 1995; Jordan et al., 2007; Jordan and Newell, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting step-to-step variability in running.

claim: Step-to-step variability could be due to internal perturbative sources like muscle force noise and sensory noise.
source: This step-to-step variability could be due to internal perturbative sources like muscle force noise and sensory noise (Warren et al., 1986; Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Osborne et al., 2005) or small external perturbations (e.g. visual field inhomogeneity, small ground imperfections).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on motor and sensory noise.

claim: Step-to-step variability could be due to small external perturbations such as visual field inhomogeneity and small ground imperfections.
source: This step-to-step variability could be due to internal perturbative sources like muscle force noise and sensory noise (Warren et al., 1986; Harris and Wolpert, 1998; Osborne et al., 2005) or small external perturbations (e.g. visual field inhomogeneity, small ground imperfections).
evidence: Examples of external perturbations are provided as potential sources of variability.

claim: Deviations in the center of mass motion predict the corrective strategies during the next stance, well in advance of foot touchdown.
source: Deviations in the center of mass motion predict the corrective strategies during the next stance, well in advance of foot touchdown.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data and analysis presented.

claim: Horizontal motion is stabilized by total leg impulse modulations.
source: Horizontal motion is stabilized by total leg impulse modulations, whereas the vertical motion is stabilized by differentially modulating the impulse within stance.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data and regression analyses.

claim: Vertical motion is stabilized by differentially modulating the impulse within stance.
source: Horizontal motion is stabilized by total leg impulse modulations, whereas the vertical motion is stabilized by differentially modulating the impulse within stance.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data and regression analyses.

claim: The human-derived control strategies implemented on a simple computational biped allow it to run stably for hundreds of steps despite incessant noise-like perturbations or larger discrete perturbations.
source: We implement these human-derived control strategies on a simple computational biped, showing that it runs stably for hundreds of steps despite incessant noise-like perturbations or larger discrete perturbations.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through computational simulations described in the Results section.

claim: The running controller derived from natural variability echoes behaviors observed in previous animal and robot studies.
source: This running controller derived from natural variability echoes behaviors observed in previous animal and robot studies.
evidence: This is stated as a finding that connects the current work to prior literature.

claim: The classic modeling paradigm for running control assumes that the human leg behaves like a linear spring.
source: One classic modeling paradigm for running control assumes that the human leg behaves like a linear spring (Blickhan, 1989; McMahon and Cheng, 1990; Blickhan and Full, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on spring-mass models of running.

claim: Spring-mass running models have been used to argue how passive-elastic properties may reduce muscle work needed for locomotion.
source: This paradigm has been used to argue how passive-elastic properties may reduce muscle work needed for locomotion (Alexander and Vernon, 1975; Alexander, 1990) and has been useful in examining locomotion in a simplified setting.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on the role of elastic properties in locomotion.

claim: Variants of spring-mass running models have demonstrated stable running.
source: Variants of these spring-mass running models have demonstrated stable running (Seyfarth et al., 2002; Seipel and Holmes, 2005; Ghigliazza et al., 2005; Geyer et al., 2006; Srinivasan and Holmes, 2008; Englsberger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on stable running models.

claim: Spring-mass models have been successful in fitting the average center of mass motion during running.
source: These models have been successful in fitting the average center of mass motion during running (Blickhan and Full, 1993; Geyer et al., 2006; Srinivasan and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature demonstrating model fits to data.

claim: Understanding running stability requires understanding how deviations from the average motion are controlled.
source: However, understanding running stability requires understanding how deviations from the average motion are controlled.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement that motivates the study's approach.

claim: Spring-like leg mechanics cannot explain how deviations from the average motion are controlled and eventually attenuated.
source: It has been previously recognized that spring-like leg mechanics cannot explain how deviations from the average motion are controlled and eventually attenuated (e.g. Ghigliazza et al., 2005; Biewener and Daley, 2007; Maus et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature recognizing limitations of spring-mass models.

claim: The only way to control the center of mass motion is for the leg to systematically change the forces and the impulses it applies on the ground.
source: The only way to control the center of mass motion is for the leg to systematically change the forces and the impulses it applies on the ground.
evidence: This follows from Newton's laws of motion and is a fundamental principle of mechanics.

claim: Eight subjects (three female and five male) participated in the running experiments.
source: Eight subjects, three female and five male (age 25.0 ±5 years, weight 66.8 ±7 kg, height 1.8 ±0.14 m, leg length 1.05 ±0.08 m, mean ± s.d.) ran on a split-belt treadmill at three constant speeds: 2.5, 2.7 and 2.9 m/s, presented in random order.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and participants.

claim: Subjects ran at three constant speeds: 2.5, 2.7 and 2.9 m/s.
source: Eight subjects, three female and five male (age 25.0 ±5 years, weight 66.8 ±7 kg, height 1.8 ±0.14 m, leg length 1.05 ±0.08 m, mean ± s.d.) ran on a split-belt treadmill at three constant speeds: 2.5, 2.7 and 2.9 m/s, presented in random order.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: Each speed had 2075 ± 67 strides across all subjects with subjects running about 3.5 min on average.
source: Each speed had 2075 ± 67 strides across all subjects (one stride = two steps) with subjects running about 3.5 min on average.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: The control in the fore-aft and sideways directions are independent or decoupled.
source: Thus, it appears that the control in the fore-aft and sideways directions are independent or decoupled.
evidence: This is inferred from the regression analysis showing minimal coupling between directions.

claim: Humans exhibit a 'one-step dead-beat controller' on average for sideways velocity deviations.
source: But humans seem to exhibit a 'one-step dead-beat controller' on average for sideways velocity deviations (the term deadbeat control refers to when state deviations decay to zero in a finite amount of time).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression coefficient from the experimental data.

claim: All eigenvalues of the apex-to-apex map matrix product were less than one in absolute value, indicating a stable periodic motion.
source: The eigenvalues of this matrix product were all less than one in absolute value, indicating a stable periodic motion.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the eigenvalue analysis indicating stability.

claim: The net vertical impulse between two consecutive flight apexes is zero.
source: A flight apex occurs when the center of mass vertical velocity is zero. So, the net vertical impulse between two consecutive flight apexes is also zero (as it equals the change in vertical momentum, according to the impulse-momentum equation).
evidence: This follows from the impulse-momentum theorem and the definition of flight apex.

claim: Changing the net vertical impulse over a stance phase will not accomplish any meaningful control in the vertical direction.
source: Therefore, changing the net vertical impulse over a stance phase will not accomplish any meaningful control in the vertical direction.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the impulse-momentum considerations.

claim: A downward position deviation at flight apex results in landing with a shorter leg length than nominal.
source: Thus, a downward position deviation at flight apex would result in landing with a shorter leg length than nominal (e.g. via flexed knee or ankle).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression result for landing leg length.

claim: A downward position deviation is analogous to a sudden step-up perturbation, so reducing the landing leg length reduces trip likelihood.
source: A downward position deviation is analogous to a sudden step-up perturbation, so reducing the landing leg length reduces trip likelihood.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the landing leg length control strategy.

claim: A sideways velocity perturbation to the body results in the foot being placed further along the direction of the perturbation.
source: That is, a sideways velocity perturbation to the body results in the foot being placed further along the direction of the perturbation. So, a rightward perturbation results in a more rightward step.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the foot placement regression results.

claim: A forward velocity perturbation results in the foot being placed further forward relative to the body.
source: Analogously, a forward velocity perturbation results in the foot being placed further forward relative to the body.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the foot placement regression results.

claim: There is no significant coupling between sideways and fore-aft directions in foot placement control.
source: As with the impulses, again, there is no significant coupling between sideways and fore-aft directions.
evidence: This is an observation from the regression analysis showing independent control.

claim: Less than 10% of the eventual foot placement is predicted by the swing foot at the beginning of flight phase.
source: Less than 10% of the eventual foot placement is predicted by the swing foot at the beginning of flight phase (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase-dependent regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Most swing foot re-positioning may happen during the flight phase.
source: The explanatory power of the swing foot rises rapidly during the flight phase from less than 10% to a 100% when it becomes the next stance foot, suggesting that most swing foot re-positioning may happen during this flight phase.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase-dependent regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: At the beginning of flight phase, the center of mass state is a vastly better predictor of the next foot placement than the swing foot itself.
source: At the beginning of flight phase (and earlier), the center of mass state is a vastly better predictor of the next foot placement than the swing foot itself (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the phase-dependent regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The center of mass state can predict foot placement better than the relative swing foot state until about 100 ms before foot touchdown.
source: We can predict the foot placement using the center of mass state better than just the relative swing foot state until about 100 ms before foot touchdown.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the phase-dependent regression analysis.

claim: The explanatory power of the center of mass remains flat during flight.
source: The explanatory power of the center of mass remains flat during flight.
evidence: This is an observation from the phase-dependent regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The flatness of center of mass explanatory power during flight is likely because center of mass state follows a parabolic path during flight and thus accumulates no new variation.
source: This flatness is likely because center of mass state follows a parabolic path during flight and thus accumulates no new variation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation about center of mass explanatory power.

claim: The runners did not prioritize controlling their position relative to the treadmill (station-keeping).
source: Thus, the runners did not prioritize controlling their position relative to the treadmill (station-keeping).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression results showing minimal effect of absolute position.

claim: The running control gains have approximate bilateral (left-right) symmetry.
source: The running control gains have approximate bilateral (left-right) symmetry.
evidence: This is an observation from the regression analysis comparing left and right leg control.

claim: Gains that couple sideways direction variables and either fore-aft or vertical direction variables have mirror-symmetry.
source: The gains that couple sideways direction variables and either fore-aft or vertical direction variables have mirror-symmetry (see Equations 1,2,8,9).
evidence: This is an observation from the regression analysis comparing left and right leg control.

claim: Gains that couple one sideways variable with another sideways variable, or one fore-aft variable with another fore-aft variable, are the same for the left and right legs without any sign changes.
source: On the other hand, gains that couple one sideways variable with another sideways variable, or one fore-aft variable with another fore-aft variable, are the same for the left and right legs without any such sign changes.
evidence: This is an observation from the regression analysis comparing left and right leg control.

claim: The mirror symmetry in running control likely follows from the approximate mirror symmetry in body physiology about the sagittal plane.
source: This mirror symmetry in running control likely follows from the approximate mirror symmetry in body physiology about the sagittal plane and was also found in walking (Wang and Srinivasan, 2014; Ankaralı et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the symmetry observation, supported by citations to similar findings in walking.

claim: The symmetry suggests the lack of a substantially dominant limb for running control.
source: This symmetry suggests the lack of a substantially dominant limb for running control, in contrast to the asymmetry and limb role differentiation that occurs in some other tasks (Peters, 1988).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the symmetry observation, contrasted with other tasks.

claim: The simple biped models' ground reaction forces are similar to experimental data despite not explicitly matching the curves.
source: We find that the models' ground reaction forces are similar to experimental data despite not explicitly matching the curves (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The phase-dependent ground reaction force feedback gains for the models are qualitatively similar to the phase-dependent gains inferred from experiment.
source: Further, we find that the phase-dependent ground reaction force feedback gains for the models are qualitatively similar to the phase-dependent gains inferred from experiment (Figure 8b), again, despite not explicitly fitting the shape of these phase-dependent gains.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The simple models can capture not only the average motion during running, but also how the runner responds to deviations from the average motion.
source: This shows that these simple models can not only capture the average motion during running, but also how the runner responds to deviations from the average motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulation results.

claim: The simple models' running motions are not stable without the controller.
source: The simple models' running motions are not stable without the controller: an arbitrarily small perturbation makes it diverge from the original running motion.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations.

claim: With the foot placement and leg force controller turned on, the running motion is asymptotically stable.
source: With the foot placement and leg force controller turned on, the running motion is asymptotically stable.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations.

claim: A stable periodic motion that can reject perturbations at one phase can reject perturbations at any phase.
source: It is a mathematical theorem that a stable periodic motion that can reject perturbations at one phase (say, flight apex) can reject perturbations at any phase (Guckenheimer and Holmes, 2013).
evidence: This is a mathematical theorem cited from the literature.

claim: The model rejects perturbations at any phase.
source: So, it follows that our model rejects perturbations at any phase.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the mathematical theorem and the model's stability at flight apex.

claim: A sideways or fore-aft push to the model results in convergence to the nominal running motion, except for a sideways or fore-aft position offset.
source: A sideways or fore-aft push to the model results in convergence to the nominal running motion, except for a sideways or fore-aft position offset (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations shown in Figure 9c.

claim: All positive perturbations to sideways velocity, fore-aft velocity, and vertical position result in net negative work on the first step after the perturbation.
source: All such positive perturbations result in net negative work on the first step after the perturbation, reflected in the work-loops with net negative area within them.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations shown in Figure 10.

claim: Net positive or negative leg work is necessary to recover from perturbations that change the total mechanical energy of the runner.
source: Such net positive or negative leg work is clearly necessary to recover from perturbations that change the total mechanical energy of the runner, as was recognized in prior discussions of the energy-neutral spring-mass model of running (Ghigliazza et al., 2005; Biewener and Daley, 2007; Srinivasan and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: While the direct leg force control model falls down with noise, the runner with muscles does not fall down for hundreds of steps despite the noise.
source: We find that while the direct leg force control model falls down, the runner with muscles does not fall down for hundreds of steps despite the noise.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations with noise.

claim: The variability in the center of mass state at flight apex for the model as a result of the simulated noisy control is qualitatively similar to the variability found in experiment.
source: The variability in the center of mass state at flight apex for the model (Figure 11b) as a result of the simulated noisy control is qualitatively similar to the variability found in experiment (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a comparison between model simulations and experimental data shown in Figures 11b and 2a.

claim: The model is able to run without falling despite vertical position perturbations at flight apex, which are equivalent to uneven terrain.
source: The model is also able to run without falling despite vertical position perturbations at flight apex, which are equivalent to uneven terrain.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations.

claim: Even though the model was derived using data on horizontal ground, it is capable of running robustly on uneven terrain.
source: Thus, even though the model was derived using data on horizontal ground, it is capable of running robustly on uneven terrain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model's ability to handle vertical position perturbations.

claim: The muscle-driven model is robust to motor noise presumably because of the intrinsic stabilizing properties of force-length and force-velocity relations.
source: The muscle-driven model is robust to motor noise presumably because of the intrinsic stabilizing properties of force-length and force-velocity relations (Hogan, 1984; Jindrich and Full, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model's robustness, supported by citations to literature on muscle properties.

claim: Humans use foot placement control in a manner that they step in the direction of the perturbation, thereby directing the leg force so as to oppose the perturbation.
source: We have shown that humans use foot placement or leg angle control in a manner that they step in the direction of the perturbation, thereby directing the leg force so as to oppose the perturbation.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on foot placement control.

claim: The foot placement controller derived from running data is qualitatively similar to the classic Raibert-like controller used in early running robots.
source: The foot placement controller derived from running data is qualitatively similar to the classic Raibert-like controller used in early running robots (Raibert, 1986) in that the foot placement opposes velocity deviations with no sideways-fore-aft coupling, but differs in that it has a dependence on vertical position perturbations.
evidence: This is a comparison between the study's findings and prior robotic control strategies.

claim: Humans use similar foot placement control in walking, stepping in the direction of the perturbation.
source: Humans use similar foot placement control in walking, stepping in the direction of the perturbation (Hof et al., 2010; Wang and Srinivasan, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior findings in walking, supported by citations.

claim: Appropriate foot placement is used in running ostriches while turning.
source: Previous work had shown that appropriate foot placement is used in running ostriches while turning (Jindrich et al., 2007), running humans in cutting maneuvers (Besier et al., 2003), and turning while walking (Patla et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a reference to prior findings in other contexts, supported by citations.

claim: The gain relating sideways foot placement and sideways velocity deviation was about 2.5 times greater than the gain relating fore-aft foot placement and fore-aft velocity deviation.
source: The gain relating sideways foot placement and sideways velocity deviation was about 2.5 times greater than the gain relating fore-aft foot placement and fore-aft velocity deviation; a similar factor of 3 was found in walking (Wang and Srinivasan, 2014), perhaps reflecting the greater sideways instability of a biped without foot placement control (Ghigliazza et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of control gains, with interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The recovery from a sideways perturbation is faster than from a fore-aft perturbation.
source: Also consistent with lower control authority and a greater fall propensity in the sideways direction, we find that the recovery from a sideways perturbation is faster than from a fore-aft perturbation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of perturbation recovery.

claim: Station-keeping may occur on a slower time-scale with a multi-step controller, not considered in this study.
source: While station-keeping was not prioritized over a single step, it may occur on a slower time-scale with a multi-step controller, not considered here.
evidence: This is a speculation about control strategies not examined in the current study.

claim: The dominant terms in the inferred controllers are similar for all subjects.
source: Performing the regressions for data from individual subjects indicates that the dominant terms in the inferred controllers are similar for all subjects; the subject-to-subject variability in the estimated control gains are shown in Figure 12.
evidence: This is a finding from the individual subject analysis shown in Figure 12.

claim: When a runner starts at a higher-than-normal height at flight apex, or equivalently, encounters a step-down, the runner lands with a steeper leg angle.
source: Our model predicts that when a runner starts at a higher-than-normal height at flight apex, or equivalently, encounters a step-down, the runner lands with a steeper leg angle (Figure 9d).
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model shown in Figure 9d.

claim: Landing with a steeper leg angle when encountering a step-down has been observed in humans and bipedal running birds.
source: Such behavior has been observed in humans and bipedal running birds running with large unforeseen or visible step-downs (Daley and Biewener, 2006; Grimmer et al., 2008; Müller et al., 2012; Qiao and Jindrich, 2012).
evidence: This is a reference to prior experimental findings, supported by citations.

claim: Step-ups decrease touch-down angle.
source: Conversely, step-ups decrease touch-down angle, as predicted (Birn-Jeffery and Daley, 2012).
evidence: This is a reference to prior experimental findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The behavior of landing with steeper leg angle on step-downs has been attributed to swing leg retraction just before foot contact.
source: This behavior has been attributed to swing leg retraction just before foot contact (Seyfarth, 2003), but our foot placement controller captures this phenomenon despite not having explicit leg swing dynamics.
evidence: This is a reference to a prior explanation, supported by a citation, contrasted with the current study's findings.

claim: The model captures the phenomenon of steeper landing on step-downs despite not having explicit leg swing dynamics.
source: This behavior has been attributed to swing leg retraction just before foot contact (Seyfarth, 2003), but our foot placement controller captures this phenomenon despite not having explicit leg swing dynamics.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model simulations.

claim: The agreement between model predictions and large terrain perturbation experiments indicates that humans may use qualitatively similar control strategies for large external perturbations and small intrinsic perturbations.
source: This agreement indicates that humans may use qualitatively similar control strategies for large external perturbations and small intrinsic perturbations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between model predictions and prior experimental findings.

claim: Any running controller that achieves asymptotic stability will need to perform net mechanical work in response to perturbations that decrease or increase the body's mechanical energy.
source: It is expected that any running controller that achieves asymptotic stability will need to perform net mechanical work in response to perturbations that decrease or increase the body's mechanical energy (Ghigliazza et al., 2005; Srinivasan and Holmes, 2008; Maus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Energy-conservative spring-like leg behavior does not allow net mechanical work and can achieve only partial asymptotic stability.
source: Energy-conservative spring-like leg behavior does not allow such net mechanical work and can achieve only partial asymptotic stability, not being able to handle energy-changing perturbations (as noted by (Ghigliazza et al., 2005)).
evidence: This is a theoretical limitation of spring-mass models, supported by a citation.

claim: Spring-mass-like steady state center of mass motion in running is due to considerable muscle action and has been termed pseudo-elastic or pseudo-compliant.
source: Indeed, it is generally thought that even the spring-mass-like steady state center of mass motion in running is due to considerable muscle action and has been termed pseudo-elastic (Ruina et al., 2005) or pseudo-compliant (McN. Alexander, 1997).
evidence: This is a reference to prior conceptual frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: Energy-optimal running movements in models with no leg springs produce similar spring-mass-like center of mass trajectories.
source: Remarkably, energy-optimal running movements in models with no leg springs produce similar spring-mass-like center of mass trajectories (Srinivasan, 2011), with leg muscles performing equal amounts of positive and negative work.
evidence: This is a reference to prior modeling work, supported by a citation.

claim: A previous article fit running data to variants of the spring-mass model, allowing the spring stiffness and spring length to change during stance.
source: A previous article (Maus et al., 2015) fit running data to variants of the spring-mass model, allowing the spring stiffness and spring length to change during stance, and showing that constant values for these parameters cannot fit running data.
evidence: This is a reference to prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Direct control of leg force or activation is perhaps more parsimonious than the simultaneous control of two variables, namely, spring stiffness and length.
source: Such direct control of leg force or activation is perhaps more parsimonious than the simultaneous control of two variables, namely, spring stiffness and length.
evidence: This is a comparison of modeling approaches, expressing a preference for parsimony.

claim: Humans modulate GRF continuously over the whole stance phase for control.
source: We have shown that humans modulate GRF continuously over the whole stance phase for control (Figure 5); Maus and colleagues (Maus et al., 2015) assumed, for simplicity, an instantaneous finite energy input at mid-stance.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 5, contrasted with prior modeling assumptions.

claim: The stabilizing responses characterized in this study are likely due to a mixture of feedforward dynamics and active neurally mediated feedback control.
source: The stabilizing responses we have characterized in this study are likely due to a mixture of feedforward dynamics and active neurally mediated feedback control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the control mechanisms underlying the observed behaviors.

claim: Typical flight phase durations are greater than or about roughly equal to the typical short- or middle- latencies in reflex or feedback loops involving vestibular or proprioceptive mechanisms.
source: Our typical flight phase durations are greater than or about roughly equal to the typical short- or middle- latencies in reflex or feedback loops involving vestibular (Fitzpatrick et al., 1994; Iles et al., 2007) or proprioceptive mechanisms (Pearson and Collins, 1993; Sinkjær et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a comparison of time scales, supported by citations to literature on neural latencies.

claim: The comparison of time scales suggests feasibility of feedback based on flight phase or late stance phase information regarding center of mass state.
source: This suggests feasibility of feedback based on flight phase or late stance phase information regarding center of mass state.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of time scales.

claim: Equivalent controllers based on the center of mass state at the end of previous stance have similar predictive ability to apex-based controllers.
source: While we have focused on the control of stance based on the previous flight apex, we have found that equivalent controllers based on the center of mass state at the end of previous stance have similar predictive ability (Figure 6), thus allowing more time for neural feedback.
evidence: This is a finding from the phase-dependent regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The lag between the information in the center of mass state and the swing foot state regarding future foot placement is about 0.1 s for sideways placement.
source: Specifically, the lag between the information in the center of mass state and the swing foot state regarding future foot placement is about 0.1 s for sideways placement and about twice that for fore-aft foot placement, suggesting sufficient time for neurally mediated feedback control of foot placement (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the phase-dependent regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The lag between the information in the center of mass state and the swing foot state regarding future foot placement is about 0.2 s for fore-aft placement.
source: Specifically, the lag between the information in the center of mass state and the swing foot state regarding future foot placement is about 0.1 s for sideways placement and about twice that for fore-aft foot placement, suggesting sufficient time for neurally mediated feedback control of foot placement (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the phase-dependent regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Center of mass state information needed for feedback control could be estimated by the nervous system by integrating sensory signals from vision, proprioceptive sensors, and vestibular sensors.
source: Center of mass state or other body state information needed for feedback control could be estimated by the nervous system by integrating sensory signals from vision (Patla, 1997), proprioceptive sensors (especially when the foot is on the ground (Sainburg et al., 1995)), and vestibular sensors (Angelaki and Cullen, 2008), potentially in combination with predictive internal models (Wolpert et al., 1995; Cullen, 2004).
evidence: This is a speculation about sensory integration mechanisms, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Most available relevant sensory information is likely used, perhaps analogous to an optimal state estimator.
source: We speculate that most available relevant sensory information is used, perhaps analogous to an optimal state estimator (Kuo, 2005; Srinivasan, 2009), and degrading one sensor may result in sensory re-weighting on a slow time-scale (Carver et al., 2006; Assländer and Peterka, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation about sensory integration, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The simple point-mass model may not capture all aspects of the running data because humans have extended feet, non-point-mass upper bodies and legs with masses.
source: Because humans have extended feet, non-point-mass upper bodies and legs with masses, the simple point-mass model may not capture all aspects of the running data (Bullimore and Burn, 2006; Srinivasan and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of model limitations, supported by citations.

claim: The study made simplifying assumptions about muscle architecture, muscle properties, and muscle activation.
source: Further, we have made simplifying assumptions about muscle architecture, muscle properties (linear force-velocity relations), and muscle activation, which are meant to capture the main qualitative dynamical features of muscles, rather than model them quantitatively precisely.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of modeling assumptions and their limitations.

claim: A linear force-velocity relation may be sufficient to produce damping-like and stabilizing muscle behavior when activated.
source: For instance, we used a linear force-velocity relation, which may be sufficient to produce damping-like and stabilizing muscle behavior when activated, but this damping behavior may be accentuated by a more realistic nonlinear force-velocity relation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the adequacy of the linear force-velocity assumption.

claim: The methods used in this study are simple and non-invasive and can be replicated to study running stability and control in other animals or other approximately periodic tasks.
source: The methods used here are simple and non-invasive: they can be replicated to study running stability and control in other animals, or indeed, other approximately periodic tasks such as flapping flight and swimming.
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the methods.

claim: These methods are suitable for analyzing differences in different populations like athletes and non-athletes, the young and the elderly, and adults with and without movement disorders.
source: These methods are suitable for analyzing differences in different populations like athletes and non-athletes, the young and the elderly, and adults with and without movement disorders.
evidence: This is a statement about potential applications of the methods.

claim: Information about control differences could be used in a rehabilitation setting to track progress from a controller in the presence of a movement disorder to a more healthy controller.
source: Once such differences are well-characterized, this information could be used, say, in a rehabilitation setting to track progress from a controller in the presence of a movement disorder to a more healthy controller, and to design rehabilitation robots that assist in this progress.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: The protocols were approved by the Ohio State University Institution Review Board and subjects participated with informed consent.
source: The protocols were approved by the Ohio State University Institution Review Board and subjects participated with informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: Three-dimensional ground reaction forces and moments on each belt of the treadmill were recorded by separate six-axis load cells at 1000 Hz.
source: Three-dimensional ground reaction forces and moments on each belt of the treadmill were recorded by separate six-axis load cells (Bertec Inc, 1000 Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection methods.

claim: Body segment motion was measured using marker-based motion capture at 100 Hz.
source: Body segment motion was measured using marker-based motion capture (Vicon T20, 100 Hz) with four reflective markers on each foot and on the torso.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection methods.

claim: To remove the slow integration drift in the center of mass velocity, a high-pass filter with a frequency cut-off equal to an eighth of mean step frequency was used.
source: To remove the slow integration drift in the center of mass velocity, we used a high-pass filter with a frequency cut-off equal to an eighth of mean step frequency (Luinge and Veltink, 2005; Schepers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methods, supported by citations.

claim: Changing the high-pass filter cut-off to a twentieth of the step frequency, or using a piecewise-linear de-trending over 20 steps, do not affect the article's conclusions.
source: Changing this high-pass filter cut-off to a twentieth of the step frequency instead, or using a piecewise-linear de-trending over 20 steps, do not affect any of this article's conclusions.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the analysis methods.

claim: Air drag was ignored because including it changed the velocities by less than 10⁻⁵ ms⁻¹, which is much smaller than the step-to-step variability.
source: We ignored air drag here, because including it changed the velocities by less than 10-5 ms-1, which is much smaller than the step-to-step variability.
evidence: This is a justification for a modeling assumption based on quantitative analysis.

claim: A weighted mean of four markers, roughly at the sacral level, was used as an approximation of the center of mass position.
source: We use a weighted mean of four markers, roughly at the sacral level, as an approximation of the center of mass position (Gard et al., 2004; Wang and Srinivasan, 2014; Perry and Srinivasan, 2017).
